evidence.title: A scientometric analysis and critical review of gas turbine aero-engines control: From Whittle engine to more-electric propulsion
evidence.abstract: The gas turbine aero-engine control systems over the past eight decades have been thoroughly investigated. This review purposes are to present a comprehensive reference for aero-engine control design and development based on a systematic scientometric analysis and to categorize different methods, algorithms, and approaches taken into account to improve the performance and operability of aircraft engines from the first days to present to enable this challenging technology to be adopted by aero-engine manufacturers. Initially, the benefits of the control systems are restated in terms of improved engine efficiency, reduced carbon dioxide emissions, and improved fuel economy. This is followed by a historical coverage of the proposed concepts dating back to 1936. A comprehensive scientometric analysis is then presented to introduce the main milestones in aero-engines control. Possible control strategies and concepts are classified into four distinct phases, including Single input- single output control algorithms, MIN-MAX or Cascade control algorithms, advanced control algorithms, More-electric and electronic control algorithms and critically reviewed. The advantages and disadvantages of milestones are discussed to cover all practical aspects of the review to enable the researchers to identify the current challenges in aircraft engine control systems.

evidence.title: A Linear LMP Model for Active and Reactive Power with Power Loss
evidence.abstract: Pricing the reactive power is more necessary than ever before because of the increasing challenge of renewable energy integration on reactive power balance and voltage control. However, reactive power price is hard to be efficiently calculated because of the non-linear nature of optimal AC power flow equation. This paper proposes a linear model to calculate active and reactive power LMP simultaneously considering power loss. Firstly, a linearized AC power flow equation is proposed based on an augmented Generation Shift Distribution Factors (GSDF) matrix. Secondly, a linearized LMP model is derived using GSDF and loss factors. The formulation of LMP is further decomposed into four components: energy, congestion, voltage limitation and power loss. Finally, an iterate algorithm is proposed for calculating LMP with the proposed model. The performance of the proposed model is validated by the IEEE-118 bus system.

evidence.title: Dynamic State Estimation for Integrated Natural Gas and Electric Power Systems
evidence.abstract: A dynamic state estimation method of integrated natural gas and electric power systems (IGESs) in proposed. Firstly, the coupling model of gas pipeline networks and power systems by gas turbine units (GTUs) is established. Secondly, the Kalman filter based linear DSE model for the IGES is built. The gas density and mass flow rate, as well as the real and imaginary parts of bus voltages are taken as states, which are predicted by the linearized fluid dynamic equations of gases and exponential smoothing techniques. Boundary conditions of pipeline networks are used as supplementary constraints in the system model. At last, the proposed method is applied to an IGES including a 30-node pipeline network and IEEE 39-bus system coupled by two GTUs. Two indexes are used to evaluate the DSE performance under three measurement error conditions, and the results show that the DSE can obtain the accurate dynamic states in different conditions.

evidence.title: Real-time Power System Simulation with Hardware Devices through DNP3 in Cyber-Physical Testbed
evidence.abstract: Modern power grids are dependent on communication systems for data collection, visualization, and control. Distributed Network Protocol 3 (DNP3) is commonly used in supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) systems in power systems to allow control system software and hardware to communicate. To study the dependencies between communication network security, power system data collection, and industrial hardware, it is important to enable communication capabilities with real-time power system simulation. In this paper, we present the integration of new functionality of a power systems dynamic simulation package into our cyber-physical power system testbed that supports real-time power system data transfer using DNP3, demonstrated with an industrial real-time automation controller (RTAC). The usage and configuration of DNP3 with real-world equipment in to achieve power system monitoring and control of a large-scale synthetic electric grid via this DNP3 communication is presented. Then, an exemplar of DNP3 data collection and control is achieved in software and hardware using the 2000-bus Texas synthetic grid.

evidence.title: Modeling and simulation enabled UAV electrical power system design
evidence.abstract: With the diversity of mission capability and the associated requirement for more advanced technologies, designing modern unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) systems is an especially challenging task. In particular, the increasing reliance on the electrical power system for delivering key aircraft functions, both electrical and mechanical, requires that a systems-approach be employed in their development. A key factor in this process is the use of modeling and simulation to inform upon critical design choices made. However, effective systems-level simulation of complex UAV power systems presents many challenges, which must be addressed to maximize the value of such methods. This paper presents the initial stages of a power system design process for a medium altitude long endurance (MALE) UAV focusing particularly on the development of three full candidate architecture models and associated technologies. The unique challenges faced in developing such a suite of models and their ultimate role in the design process is explored, with case studies presented to reinforce key points. The role of the developed models in supporting the design process is then discussed

abstract.value: A dynamic state estimation method of integrated natural gas and electric power systems (IGESs) in proposed. Firstly, the coupling model of gas pipeline networks and power systems by gas turbine units (GTUs) is established. Secondly, the Kalman filter based linear DSE model for the IGES is built. The gas density and mass flow rate, as well as the real and imaginary parts of bus voltages are taken as states, which are predicted by the linearized fluid dynamic equations of gases and exponential smoothing techniques. Boundary conditions of pipeline networks are used as supplementary constraints in the system model. At last, the proposed method is applied to an IGES including a 30-node pipeline network and IEEE 39-bus system coupled by two GTUs. Two indexes are used to evaluate the DSE performance under three measurement error conditions, and the results show that the DSE can obtain the accurate dynamic states in different conditions.

system.value: Real-time Power System Simulation with Hardware Devices through DNP3 in Cyber-Physical Testbed

abstract.value: Modern power grids are dependent on communication systems for data collection, visualization, and control. Distributed Network Protocol 3 (DNP3) is commonly used in supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) systems in power systems to allow control system software and hardware to communicate. To study the dependencies between communication network security, power system data collection, and industrial hardware, it is important to enable communication capabilities with real-time power system simulation. In this paper, we present the integration of new functionality of a power systems dynamic simulation package into our cyber-physical power system testbed that supports real-time power system data transfer using DNP3, demonstrated with an industrial real-time automation controller (RTAC). The usage and configuration of DNP3 with real-world equipment in to achieve power system monitoring and control of a large-scale synthetic electric grid via this DNP3 communication is presented. Then, an exemplar of DNP3 data collection and control is achieved in software and hardware using the 2000-bus Texas synthetic grid.

system.value: Modeling and simulation enabled UAV electrical power system design

abstract.value: With the diversity of mission capability and the associated requirement for more advanced technologies, designing modern unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) systems is an especially challenging task. In particular, the increasing reliance on the electrical power system for delivering key aircraft functions, both electrical and mechanical, requires that a systems-approach be employed in their development. A key factor in this process is the use of modeling and simulation to inform upon critical design choices made. However, effective systems-level simulation of complex UAV power systems presents many challenges, which must be addressed to maximize the value of such methods. This paper presents the initial stages of a power system design process for a medium altitude long endurance (MALE) UAV focusing particularly on the development of three full candidate architecture models and associated technologies. The unique challenges faced in developing such a suite of models and their ultimate role in the design process is explored, with case studies presented to reinforce key points. The role of the developed models in supporting the design process is then discussed

warnings.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-016 (sharpened per CEO Round 58): A proposed latent quantity survives only when (1) identifiability is demonstrated under an EXPLICIT observation/dynamics model with full rank/observability analysis (not naive unknown-count), AND (2) identifiability REMAINS under plausible model uncertainty (each ideal assumption relaxed toward realistic physics and re-tested). warnings.mechanism: Capability collision test — keyword collision search is insufficient to establish novelty
warnings.lesson:
FROZEN THEOREM CE-018: A novelty claim survives only when the candidate's CAPABILITY (what it can DO) is demonstrably absent from the prior art landscape — not when the candidate's KEYWORDS (what words it uses) are absent. The correct procedure: (1) decompose the candidate into its functional capabilities (e.g., 'intrapprocedural clot sensing' not 'retrieved-clot physical signature measurement'); (2) search the prior art landscape for each capability using the prior art's own vocabulary (assignee names, CPC classes, commercial product names, inventor terminology); (3) build a capability collision matrix mapping each capability to prior art coverage; (4) only if at least one capability is genuinely UNOCCUPIED (confirmed by both patent search AND commercial frontier analysis) can a novelty claim be recorded. Semantic re-skins (CE-012 violation) include: 'retrieved-clot' vs 'in-situ clot'; 'physical signature' vs 'composition'; 'integrated sensor' vs 'catheter-mounted sensor.' These distinctions prove nothing. The test is capability, not vocabulary.

SHARPENED (per CEO Round 62 audit): Capability novelty must be evaluated at the FUNCTIONAL END-TO-END level: input → inference → decision → physical effect → measurable outcome. Otherwise the machine can still find a 'novel' intermediate layer (e.g., a new sensor modality, a new feature, a new algorithm) that is already covered by an existing end-to-end system. The correct end-to-end test: (5) decompose the candidate into the complete causal loop — what is observed → what is inferred → what is predicted → what physical action becomes possible → what measurable outcome changes; (6) map each step of this loop to the prior art's end-to-end systems (not just individual capabilities); (7) only if the candidate's complete causal loop is demonstrably absent from the prior art's end-to-end systems can a novelty claim be recorded. A 'novel' intermediate layer that plugs into an existing end-to-end system is NOT novel — it is a substitution, not an invention. The unit of novelty is the complete causal loop, not the sensor, feature, algorithm, or capability.

informational.mechanism: RES-4 narrow: adaptive transverse/sigmoid sinus stent for CSF absorption regulation via AG pressure gradient control
informational.lesson: MODEL-BOUNDED NEGATIVE RESULT: Before inventing variable geometry, calculate absolute pressure-control authority at the actual operating point. Relative r^4 sensitivity is meaningless if the absolute pressure drop is tiny. Under realistic post-stenting conditions (D=5-10mm, Q=200-500 mL/min), adaptive diameter control of a venous sinus produces <0.2 mmHg change in AG gradient — 5x below the 1 mmHg pre-registered threshold. Control authority exists only in the stenotic+high-flow regime (D≤4mm, Q≥1200 mL/min), which is incompatible with a stented patient whose stent has normalized diameter to 7-10mm. The network model (1323 configs) confirms: flow redistribution through contralateral sinus does NOT rescue control authority (dominance has no effect). NOT a universal vascular invariant — based on Poiseuille model with specific assumptions about geometry, flow, and topology.

informational.mechanism: Minimum Sufficient Validation Evidence Derivation (MSVED) — 4-link chain: ML change → clinical pathway → risk envelope → minimum sufficient evidence → sufficiency proof
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-019: A clinical-pathway-aware evidence selector must demonstrate that the clinical-pathway bridge produces a MATERIALLY DIFFERENT and BETTER evidence set than information-maximizing selection (BOED). If the pathway-aware selector uses MORE tests while achieving WORSE assurance, the clinical-pathway bridge adds complexity without value. The minimum-evidence claim must be validated by showing tests_required < BOED, not just tests_required < conventional. The killer experiment must compare against the STRONGEST available baseline (BOED), not just conventional full-validation.

informational.mechanism: Automated Sufficiency Proof Generator (CC-04 / MSES theorem) — formal proof that a specific evidence set E is sufficient to establish modification-specific clinical risk envelope R(Δ)
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-020: A sufficiency proof that is merely an integration of known statistical methods (NI testing + coverage + multiple-testing correction + sensitivity analysis) is NOT a novel mathematical result. Under §103, combining known methods to solve a problem the market explicitly asks for is likely obvious (KSR v. Teleflex). The frontier is a NEW MATHEMATICAL BOUND — e.g., a tight bound on minimum evidence set size that is better than what existing methods give individually, or a proof technique that connects clinical pathway coverage to statistical sufficiency in a way that is not derivable from existing theory. Additionally: killer tests for sufficiency proofs must include a TRUE POSITIVE case (sufficient evidence for a SAFE modification that the system correctly accepts), not just a true negative (insufficient evidence that the system correctly rejects).

informational.mechanism: Non-Inferiority Statistical Engine (CC-08) — automated paired NI comparison with pre-registered margins for ML model modifications
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-021: Automating a standard statistical test (NI testing) for a regulatory context that explicitly requires it (PCCP) is NOT an invention. Under KSR, combining known methods to solve a problem the market explicitly asks for is obvious. The coder correctly identified this in the R254 ranking ("NI testing is standard, high collision risk") but incorrectly chose to proceed. The CEO corrected: high collision risk is a RED FLAG, not a reason to proceed. Kill immediately if the smallest surviving mechanism is standard statistics + ML context + automated reporting.

informational.mechanism: SGET (Strain-Gated Electrochemical Transduction) — A=strain pulse changes B=electrochemical sensor from 2D surface to 3D depth profiling. First synergy-2 candidate.
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-022: Synergy ≠ novelty and synergy ≠ commercial moat. A functional interaction (A changes B) is NECESSARY but NOT SUFFICIENT for invention. The interaction itself — the causal law, the emergent effect, and functional equivalents across domains — must survive prior art independently. Additionally: synergy claims without quantitative comparison against the STRONGEST baseline are stories, not evidence. The unexpected-effect proof requires: (1) pre-registered quantitative prediction, (2) strongest baseline identified, (3) killer experiment vs that baseline, (4) result not predictable from A and B independently. The new standard: A changes B → unexpected effect → interaction survives prior art → reproducible advantage → cannot be cheaply reproduced → buyer value.

informational.mechanism: SC-05 Biofilm-Resistant Living-Surface Venous Interface — continuously renewing anti-biofilm surface with active surface-energy control at CSF-blood interface
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-023: A candidate that survives the 14-gate protocol at the CONCEPT level can be killed at the ELEMENT-DECOMPOSITION level. The 14 gates assessed M4 against the broad concept (continuously renewing anti-biofilm surface) and found M4=NOT FOUND. But deep collision revealed that each element (continuous renewal, dynamic topography, surface-energy modulation) is individually occupied by prior art. The combination is an aggregation of known anti-fouling approaches. The lesson: M4 must be assessed at the ELEMENT level, not the concept level. And M4=NOT FOUND means the search has not found comparable performance yet — not that it does not exist.

custody_records.raw_content: The gas turbine aero-engine control systems over the past eight decades have been thoroughly investigated. This review purposes are to present a comprehensive reference for aero-engine control design and development based on a systematic scientometric analysis and to categorize different methods, algorithms, and approaches taken into account to improve the performance and operability of aircraft engines from the first days to present to enable this challenging technology to be adopted by aero-engine manufacturers. Initially, the benefits of the control systems are restated in terms of improved engine efficiency, reduced carbon dioxide emissions, and improved fuel economy. This is followed by a historical coverage of the proposed concepts dating back to 1936. A comprehensive scientometric analysis is then presented to introduce the main milestones in aero-engines control. Possible control strategies and concepts are classified into four distinct phases, including Single input- single output control algorithms, MIN-MAX or Cascade control algorithms, advanced control algorithms, More-electric and electronic control algorithms and critically reviewed. The advantages and disadvantages of milestones are discussed to cover all practical aspects of the review to enable the researchers to identify the current challenges in aircraft engine control systems.

custody_records.raw_content: Pricing the reactive power is more necessary than ever before because of the increasing challenge of renewable energy integration on reactive power balance and voltage control. However, reactive power price is hard to be efficiently calculated because of the non-linear nature of optimal AC power flow equation. This paper proposes a linear model to calculate active and reactive power LMP simultaneously considering power loss. Firstly, a linearized AC power flow equation is proposed based on an augmented Generation Shift Distribution Factors (GSDF) matrix. Secondly, a linearized LMP model is derived using GSDF and loss factors. The formulation of LMP is further decomposed into four components: energy, congestion, voltage limitation and power loss. Finally, an iterate algorithm is proposed for calculating LMP with the proposed model. The performance of the proposed model is validated by the IEEE-118 bus system.

custody_records.raw_content: A dynamic state estimation method of integrated natural gas and electric power systems (IGESs) in proposed. Firstly, the coupling model of gas pipeline networks and power systems by gas turbine units (GTUs) is established. Secondly, the Kalman filter based linear DSE model for the IGES is built. The gas density and mass flow rate, as well as the real and imaginary parts of bus voltages are taken as states, which are predicted by the linearized fluid dynamic equations of gases and exponential smoothing techniques. Boundary conditions of pipeline networks are used as supplementary constraints in the system model. At last, the proposed method is applied to an IGES including a 30-node pipeline network and IEEE 39-bus system coupled by two GTUs. Two indexes are used to evaluate the DSE performance under three measurement error conditions, and the results show that the DSE can obtain the accurate dynamic states in different conditions.

custody_records.raw_content: Modern power grids are dependent on communication systems for data collection, visualization, and control. Distributed Network Protocol 3 (DNP3) is commonly used in supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) systems in power systems to allow control system software and hardware to communicate. To study the dependencies between communication network security, power system data collection, and industrial hardware, it is important to enable communication capabilities with real-time power system simulation. In this paper, we present the integration of new functionality of a power systems dynamic simulation package into our cyber-physical power system testbed that supports real-time power system data transfer using DNP3, demonstrated with an industrial real-time automation controller (RTAC). The usage and configuration of DNP3 with real-world equipment in to achieve power system monitoring and control of a large-scale synthetic electric grid via this DNP3 communication is presented. Then, an exemplar of DNP3 data collection and control is achieved in software and hardware using the 2000-bus Texas synthetic grid.

custody_records.raw_content: With the diversity of mission capability and the associated requirement for more advanced technologies, designing modern unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) systems is an especially challenging task. In particular, the increasing reliance on the electrical power system for delivering key aircraft functions, both electrical and mechanical, requires that a systems-approach be employed in their development. A key factor in this process is the use of modeling and simulation to inform upon critical design choices made. However, effective systems-level simulation of complex UAV power systems presents many challenges, which must be addressed to maximize the value of such methods. This paper presents the initial stages of a power system design process for a medium altitude long endurance (MALE) UAV focusing particularly on the development of three full candidate architecture models and associated technologies. The unique challenges faced in developing such a suite of models and their ultimate role in the design process is explored, with case studies presented to reinforce key points. The role of the developed models in supporting the design process is then discussed
